content.title: Mortgage rates drop to 1-year low: Why experts say lock in now or risk paying more
content.text: If you’re house hunting right now, you're likely navigating through excitement and uncertainty. Mortgage rates just hit their lowest levels in a year, and recent data shows a clear shift toward buyers across the U.S. housing market. However, the mortgage market remains a dynamic environment where rates still fluctuate daily, and more critical economic data is due in the next few weeks. What if you miss out on a good deal?This is where mortgage rate locks come into play. A rate lock is a tool that enables you to prevent rates from fluctuating before you close. As you shop around for a new home loan, here’s how a mortgage rate lock works and when it could make sense for your next purchase or mortgage refinance.⭐️ Must read: 4 popular mortgage loans for homebuyers: Conventional, FHA, VA and jumbo loansWhat is a mortgage rate lock?A mortgage rate lock is a guarantee from your lender that your interest rate won't change for a set period of time — often 30 to 60 days or longer. Also called a lock-in, it allows you to do just that: lock in today's rates to protect you from market fluctuations during the homebuying or refinance process.Did you know?If you don't lock in your rate, you're "floating" it. This means your final rate could end up higher or lower than today's rates, depending on financial market changes before your loan closes.🔍 Learn more: How to shop for a mortgage: A guide for homebuyers in 2025How does a mortgage rate lock work?Locking in your rate shields you from the impact of the ups and downs of interest rates. Your lender is obligated to honor the rate they promised you, even if market conditions shift, as long as your application has no major changes.Rate locks can provide crucial financial stability to all kinds of buyers or homeowners, especially those on fixed incomes or retirees. "Locking in a mortgage rate is really about keeping things steady and secure, especially when you're on a fixed income,” says Matt Schwartz, mortgage broker and founder of the VA Loan Network. “I've had clients in their 60s who locked in a rate just before they spiked, and it saved them a lot on monthly payments.”For example, if you lock in a 6% interest rate for 45 days and rates jump to 6.5% a week later, you're still guaranteed a 6% rate. On a conventional 30-year, $400,000 mortgage, that’s the equivalent of saving $41,120 in interest over the life of your loan.However, if rates fall to 5.5% while you have a rate lock for 6%, you might feel like you missed out. That’s why some lenders offer a float-down option.Should I look into a float-down option?A float-down option is like an insurance policy on your rate lock. If borrower rates decrease during your rate lock period, you can "float down" to the lower interest rate.This feature usually comes with a fee that can range from 0.25% to 1% of your mortgage amount, depending on the lender. But the potential savings can be worth it if interest rates are falling, like after Fed rate cuts expected next month. Your lender can tell you if it offers a float-down option and what the terms are.🔍 Learn more: How to get the lowest rate on your next mortgage: Expert tips for lower costsHow to lock in your mortgage rateMost homebuyers choose to lock their rate after their offer has been accepted and they've applied for their loan. At this point, you usually have a property address and a clear idea of your closing date. This is important because you want your rate lock to last through closing. "A lot of people don't realize rate locks don't last forever," says Schwartz. "You have to pay attention to the expiration date." You’ll usually follow these steps to lock in your rate:Get preapproved for a mortgage. Gather your personal and financial information, and apply for preapproval with a lender.Find your dream home and make an offer. Work with a real estate agent or draw up your offer letter on your own, and then put down your earnest money deposit.Submit your loan application. After your officer is accepted, you can apply with the lender that preapproved you, or apply with several lenders to compare the interest rates, APRs, loan terms and closing costs.Choose a lender and lock in your rate. Note the length of your mortgage rate lock to ensure it covers you through your closing date.Close on your new home. Sign the final paperwork and get your keys to your new home!Can I switch lenders after locking in a mortgage rate?Yes, but you risk losing your earnest money and potentially the house you're interested in. Applying with a new lender resets the time needed to confirm your creditworthiness and financials, setting you back by a month or more. In a tight market, it's possible a new homebuyer could swoop in with a more attractive offer in that time. Think carefully about any benefits of switching so late in the homebuying process, and talk with a trusted real estate agent or financial advisor if you're not sure how to proceed.🔍 Learn more: Prequalification vs. preapproval: How to time these two tools when shopping for a mortgageHow much do rate locks cost?You’ll usually pay 0.25% to 1% of your loan amount for a rate lock, depending on the lender. On a $400,000 mortgage loan, that’s the equivalent of paying from $1,000 to $4,000.Generally, the longer you want to lock in your rate, the more it will cost. For a 30-day rate lock, you might pay as little as 0.25%. If you want to lock in your rate for 60 days or more, the cost could climb to 2% of your loan.We talked about how locking in a 6% rate instead of a 6.5% rate on a $400,000, 30-year mortgage could save you $51,120 over the life of the loan. In this scenario, even paying $4,000 for a rate lock would still leave you with a net savings of $47,120.Some mortgage lenders offer “free” rate locks. But the cost of these free locks is often built into your loan in other ways, such as through higher origination fees or slightly higher interest rates.🔍 Learn more: What are the monthly payments on a $500,000 mortgage?When should you lock in a mortgage rate?As a rule of thumb, most experts recommend locking in your rate after your offer has been accepted and you've submitted your loan application. This is when you have a clear idea of your closing date, which is key because you want your rate lock to last through closing.If you lock in too early and closing is delayed, your rate lock could expire before you've finalized your purchase. If that happens, you might have to pay an upfront fee to extend your lock or risk getting stuck with a higher interest rate.By contrast, if you wait too long to lock and rates keep rising, you could end up paying more than you need to. It's a bit of a balancing act.Melissa Cohn, regional vice president of William Raveis Mortgage, says that choosing the right time to lock in is based on several factors:Where are rates headed? As more economic data is released and Fed rate cuts expected next month, rates could fluctuate, giving you a window of opportunity to lock in.How much time do you need? You’ll want your rate lock to get you to your expected closing date.Are there any unknowns that can impact the rate — such as a low loan-to-value (LTV) ratio, or your mortgage amount divided by the property’s value? Lenders extend the best rates for LTVs of under 80%, especially for refinancing.🔍 Learn more: When to refinance a mortgage: 4 key times when refinancing makes senseAre mortgage rate locks worth it?Rate locks may be worth it if you’re on a fixed income or buying a home in the current volatile market. At the same time, a rate lock isn't an absolute guarantee.Your lock could be voided if there are changes to your application, such as changes to:The income reported on your application.Your credit score or credit report because you opened a new account or had a late payment.Loan amount because the appraisal value came back higher or lower than expected."If you're not a fan of risk, locking in early can give you peace of mind. I've seen people try to wait for a better rate, only to miss out and end up with a higher payment,” says Schwartz. “My advice? If the rate works for you, lock it in and don't take chances with your retirement funds."🔍 Learn more:9 surprising factors that can damage your credit score (and how to fix them)Questions to ask before locking in your rateRate-lock policies vary by lender, so Cohn recommends asking these questions to protect yourself from surprises:Are you locking in for enough time to close the loan before the rate lock expires?If the rates drop, is there a float-down option?If there is a float-down option, is it free — or do you have to pay for it?If the rate lock expires before you close, what are the costs of extending the lock?🔍 Learn more: What I wish I knew before buying a house (that no realtor ever tells you)Why do mortgage rates fluctuate?Mortgage rates are influenced by the ebbs and flows of the economy, the housing market, as well as the Federal Reserve's decisions on short-term interest rates. When the Federal Reserve lowers the federal funds rate, mortgage interest rates tend to drop too. When the Fed increases rates, they tend to rise.Even global events, ranging from market conditions to geopolitical shifts, can send ripples through the mortgage market.This constant fluctuation is why timing is so important when locking in a mortgage rate. Working closely with your loan officer and real estate agent can help you seize the right moment to secure a rate that fits your budget.🔍 Learn more: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage ratesOther stories you'll likeAbout the writerCassidy Horton is a finance writer who specializes in banking, insurance, lending and paying down debt. Her expertise has been featured in NerdWallet, Forbes Advisor, MarketWatch, CNN Underscored, USA Today, Money, The Balance and Consumer Affairs, among other top financial publications. Cassidy first became interested in personal finance after paying off $18,000 in debt in 10 months of graduation with an MBA. Today, she's committed to empowering people to stand up and take charge of their financial futures.Article edited by Kelly Suzan Waggoner📩 Have thoughts or comments about this story — or ideas on topics you’d like us to cover?
